summary: This document defines HTTP fields for integrity digests. Content-Digest protects message content and Repr-Digest protects a representation. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest let a sender state its preferences. It obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest fields.

eli5.summary: When you send a package, you can add a sealed number that sums up what is inside. The receiver recomputes it to check nothing got changed or lost.

questions: what is the http content-digest header
subtitle: HTTP header fields that carry a hash of a message's content or representation, replacing the older Digest field.

tldr.problem: HTTP has no built-in way to protect the integrity of content. TCP checksums and TLS only cover a single connection, but HTTP messages often cross a chain of connections where data can be corrupted.
tldr.mechanism: Content-Digest carries a digest of the message content and Repr-Digest carries a digest of the selected representation. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest let a sender say which algorithms it prefers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9530 obsoletes RFC 3230 and its Digest and Want-Digest fields, which implementations had interpreted inconsistently.

today: RFC 9530 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 3230, so Digest and Want-Digest are marked obsoleted in the IANA field registry.

sections.title: Why HTTP Needs Integrity Fields
sections.content:
HTTP does not define a way to protect the integrity of content or representations. Lower layers help a little: TCP checksums and TLS records can detect some damage. The RFC says this is of limited use because it is opaque to the application layer and only covers a single connection, while HTTP messages often travel over a chain of separate connections.

RFC 9530 defines two digest mechanisms. Content integrity acts on the conveyed content, and representation data integrity acts on the representation data. The second supports uses such as checking a resource that was reconstructed from parts fetched over several requests or connections. An example use case given is fault detection and diagnosis across system boundaries.

The document does not define authentication, authorization or privacy.
sections.eli5: A message can be passed along through many helpers, and any of them might smudge it. These fields add a check number so the final reader can tell whether the message arrived unsmudged.

sections.title: How the Fields Fit Together
sections.content:
A sender picks a hashing algorithm, calculates a digest from some input related to the HTTP message, and sends the algorithm identifier and the digest in an HTTP field. A receiver can validate the digest. Algorithms are listed in the Hash Algorithms for HTTP Digest Fields registry.

There are four fields. Content-Digest and Repr-Digest are together called Integrity fields. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest are called Integrity preference fields.

Integrity fields are tied to the Content-Encoding and Content-Type header fields, so one resource may have several different digest values when transferred with HTTP. They apply to content or representations, not to whole HTTP messages or fields. They can be combined with mechanisms such as digital signatures; RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures is named as one example.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of check numbers: one for what is in the box as shipped, and one for the thing the box is meant to hold. There are also two ways to ask for a check number.

sections.title: Content-Digest and Repr-Digest
sections.content:
Content-Digest carries digests calculated over the actual message content. Repr-Digest carries digests calculated over the entire selected representation data. Both can appear in requests and responses, and both can be sent in a trailer section, in which case they MAY be merged into the header section.

Each is an HTTP Structured Fields Dictionary. Each key names the hashing algorithm and each value is a Byte Sequence holding an encoded version of the digest bytes. Using a Dictionary lets a sender attach several digests made with different algorithms, which could support a move away from weaker ones.

A recipient MAY ignore any or all digests. A sender MAY send a digest without knowing whether the recipient supports the algorithm, and MAY send one even if it knows the recipient will ignore it.

Because Repr-Digest works on representations, it takes account of HTTP semantics. In a state-changing request whose representation does not describe the target resource, the digest MUST be computed on the representation data. In a PATCH request the digest is computed on the patch document, while in the response it is computed on the selected representation of the patched resource. When a response carries Content-Location, the digest is computed for the resource that header identifies. The Location header does not affect it. A message with no representation data can still assert that by taking the digest of an empty string.
sections.eli5: One check number is made from the stuff in the envelope. The other is made from the thing the envelope is really about. Either way, the sender can attach several check numbers made in different ways.

sections.title: Asking for a Digest
sections.content:
A sender uses Want-Content-Digest or Want-Repr-Digest to say it would like to receive the matching Integrity field, and which algorithms it prefers. They can be used in requests and responses. In a response they tell the client that the server would like the Integrity field on future requests.

Both are Dictionaries whose keys name algorithms and whose values are Integers from 0 to 10. A value of 1 is the least preferred, 10 is the most preferred, and 0 means not acceptable. An example is Want-Repr-Digest: sha-512=3, sha-256=10, unixsum=0.

These fields are only a hint. The receiver can ignore them and send any algorithm, or no digest at all, and that is not a protocol error. The appendix shows a server answering a request for sha with sha-512, and another option where it rejects the request with an error status.
sections.eli5: It is like saying which kind of receipt you would like. The shop may hand you a different kind, and that is allowed.

sections.title: Hash Algorithms and Registration
sections.content:
Algorithms live in an IANA registry, with new entries under the Specification Required policy. Each entry has a status. Active algorithms are RECOMMENDED and can be used in adversarial settings. Deprecated algorithms are weak or lack those properties: they MAY be used against accidental corruption but MUST NOT be used in a potentially adversarial setting, such as when signing Integrity fields. Provisional is for unproven algorithms.

The initial registry has sha-512 and sha-256 as Active. The Deprecated entries are md5, sha (SHA-1), unixsum, unixcksum, adler and crc32c. Keeping the deprecated ones helps applications migrating from RFC 3230 that already store computed digests.
sections.eli5: Some ways of making a check number are strong, and some are old and easy to fool. The rules say to use the strong ones, and to use the old ones only to catch honest accidents.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Integrity fields protect representation data or content from certain kinds of corruption, but not header and trailer fields. They are not general protection against malicious tampering: an on-path attacker can remove a digest or replace it with one computed over altered data. The RFC suggests combining them with TLS or digital signatures.

When signing, a signature that covers the digest but not the representation metadata such as Content-Type can let an attacker cause a validation failure that wastes both endpoints' resources.

Other points the RFC raises:

  • Intermediaries may drop trailer fields, and content processed eagerly before a trailer digest arrives may be invalid.
  • Content codings such as gzip can produce different bytes from the same input, so the checksum cannot prove integrity at rest unless the whole content is persisted.
  • Algorithm agility does not stop downgrade or substitution attacks; a receiver relying on a digest is exposed to the weakest algorithm it accepts.
  • Validation costs computation, and skipping it to avoid exhaustion can open a downgrade attack.
sections.eli5: A check number catches honest mistakes, but a sneaky person could swap both the box and the number. To stop that you also need a lock, which is what encryption and signatures are for.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA registered Content-Digest, Repr-Digest, Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest as permanent HTTP field names, and marked Digest and Want-Digest as obsoleted. It created the Hash Algorithms for HTTP Digest Fields registry with the initial entries above.

It also deprecated the older Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Digest Algorithm Values registry. Registration there is not closed, but new registrations are encouraged to use the new registry instead.
sections.eli5: The official list of field names got four new entries and two old ones were crossed out. A new list of hash methods was started.

sections.title: Migrating from RFC 3230
sections.content:
RFC 3230 defined Digest and Want-Digest over an "instance", a term since superseded by the HTTP term "representation". Many implementations took "instance" to mean content, which caused interoperability problems. Content digests turned out to be useful too, so it was hard to tell whether such behaviour was deliberate.

The new fields separate the two cases: Repr-Digest matches what RFC 3230 intended, and Content-Digest covers what it could never express. RFC 3230 let each algorithm choose its own output encoding, giving a mix of base64, hex and decimal. Because the new fields use Structured Fields, they have a single encoding.
sections.eli5: The old rule was worded in a confusing way, so people followed it differently. The new rule uses clearer names and one way of writing the number.
